lines.trans: Do you know when you and I actually met for the very first time?
What do you mean when we first met—was it not your orientation day at KBS?
Buzzer—wrong, we met even before that! Right back there behind you—that is me.
That is seriously you?! How wild—what are the odds!
Since you lived in this neighborhood from birth and played at that playground often, we really could have crossed paths by chance!
You could even call it fate.
Oh come on, calling a background photobomb fate is a stretch!
Of course you share a longer history with Senior Joon-mo, yet even if mine with you is tiny, a thread of fate really was there.
Hey, you looked seriously adorable as a little kid!
Oh, really? Please let me keep this photo!
I wanted to thank you anyway—here, you can have it!

meanings.note: Basic verb of motion. With the respectful ending -세요 in 안녕히 가세요, it forms the polite farewell 'Goodbye!'. RR: gada.
Bound noun often contracted to 거 in everyday speech.
Honorific equivalent of 있다; used in 안녕히 계세요 ('goodbye' to someone staying).

examples.trans: Is the teacher inside right now?

meanings.note: Native Korean expression of thanks; 고마워요 is warm and polite.

examples.trans: Thank you so much for helping me.
It really is cute compared to what I thought.
Especially today, it is cute and nice.

meanings.note: refers to something known to both speakers or near the listener

그렇다.gloss: to be so, to do so

meanings.en: to be like that, to be so
meanings.note: ㅎ-irregular; also used as a pro-verb ('do so / say so')
Used as noun + -에도 (그전에도).

examples.text: 땡, 그전에도 만났어요! 여기 그 뒤에 저예요.
examples.trans: Buzzer—wrong, we met even before that! Right back there behind you—that is me.
This point about even before then is really important.

meanings.note: Colloquial contraction of 그런데; introduces a contrast or obstacle.
Used to shift the topic in conversation.

examples.trans: By the way, what time is it now?
I want to go. But I don't have time.

meanings.note: Used in spoken Korean dialogue (adj).

examples.text: 커피 시킬 때 보면 돼요, 이름 긴 거 시키는 사람들 있거든.
examples.trans: Just watch when they order coffee—some people order drinks with super long names.

meanings.note: Plain first-person singular pronoun used with friends, younger people, or subordinates; contracts to 난 with -는 and becomes 내가 before -가.

examples.trans: I'm going to stay home today.

meanings.note: Used in spoken Korean dialogue (noun).

examples.text: 술 많이 마신 날엔 밀가루 안 먹는다고 했는데 삼선짜장을 시키셔서, 어제 생각보다 많이 마신 건 아니지 않을까요?
examples.trans: He once said he avoids flour after heavy drinking yet ordered black-bean noodles—might he have drunk less than we thought?
Here the word for 'on days when' is key.

meanings.note: Used only with close friends, younger people, or children
Used colloquially for positive or negative emphasis.
Original sense of exceeding a limit.

examples.trans: The weather is so nice today.

meanings.note: Used in spoken Korean dialogue (noun).

examples.text: 이 놀이터 나 어렸을 때 옛날부터 있던 건데.
examples.trans: This playground has been right here ever since I was little.
Here the word for 'playground' is key.

meanings.note: Used in spoken Korean dialogue (noun).

examples.text: 그래서 요 며칠 내 뒤를 졸졸 따라다니면서 선배를 떠봐?
examples.trans: So that is why you trailed behind me like a puppy these past few days sounding out your senior?
Here the word for 'behind me' is key.

meanings.note: Used as game-show interjection (땡,).

examples.trans: Buzzer—wrong! I still cannot tell you.
Buzzer (wrong), it is really nice to see you.

meanings.note: Used when repeating an action.
Action of coming together with someone.

examples.trans: Today is a (of course) busy day.

meanings.note: colloquial contraction of 무엇; also used rhetorically to brush off a question

examples.trans: Why are you even asking something like that?

meanings.note: Pairs with the verb 찍다 ('to take/snap') in 사진을 찍다.

examples.trans: Shall we take a photo together?
This photo came out really well!

meanings.note: ㄹ-irregular verb: ㄹ drops before ㄴ, ㅂ, ㅅ (e.g., 사는데요, 삽니다)
Someone who started earlier than you.

examples.trans: My senior bought me a meal.

meanings.note: Bound noun used in -(으)ㄹ 수 있다/없다 ('can / cannot').
Used as plain exclamatory (신기하다,).

examples.trans: That is seriously you?! How wild—what are the odds!
It is really how amazing compared to what I expected.

meanings.note: Expresses sudden realization, surprise, or hesitation.
Negative copula used with nouns (often with -이/가)

examples.trans: Today is not Sunday, it's Monday.

meanings.note: Used in standard farewells 안녕히 계세요 and 안녕히 가세요.
ㄹ-irregular verb: stem 알- drops ㄹ before ㄴ, ㅂ, ㅅ (e.g., 압니까)

examples.trans: Do you know that person's phone number?

meanings.note: Casual exclamation used to call someone younger or a close friend.
interrogative noun asking about time; combines with particles like -부터 (from)

examples.trans: When did you come to Korea?
Since when have you worked here?

meanings.note: Often used directly without a locative particle to mean 'here'.
Used as idiomatic adverb (오다가다).

examples.text: 네가 여기서 태어나서부터 쭉 살았고 놀이터에도 자주 가고 했었으면 오다가다 만났을 수는 있었겠네 우연히!
examples.trans: Since you lived in this neighborhood from birth and played at that playground often, we really could have crossed paths by chance!
I thought it over again (in passing).
Today is a (by chance) busy day.

meanings.note: Used in spoken Korean dialogue (noun).

examples.text: 어, 너네 팀 일요일에 여기 웬일이야?
examples.trans: Oh, what brings your team here on a Sunday?
Here the word for 'what brings you?' is key.

meanings.note: demonstrative determiner placed before a noun

examples.text: 이 바닥은 자기 밥그릇은 자기가 챙겨야 돼.
examples.trans: In this industry, you have to look after your own rice bowl.

meanings.note: Everyday spoken contraction of 이것.
Used as noun + quotative + -도 (인연이라고도).

examples.trans: You could even call it fate.
Oh come on, calling a background photobomb fate is a stretch!

meanings.note: Compound of 입사 ('joining a company') + 식 ('ceremony').

examples.trans: There is an induction ceremony this morning.
Don't be late for the induction ceremony.

있다.gloss: to exist, to have, to stay

meanings.en: to exist, to be (in a place)
meanings.note: Opposite of 없다.
Marks the possessed item with 이/가.

related.gloss: to not exist, to not have

meanings.note: Used to draw attention or start an action
Indicates a high frequency of an action.
Humble first-person singular pronoun used in polite speech.
Everyday spoken intensifier; can also function as a noun meaning 'the real thing'.
Used as adverb (쭉.).

examples.text: 님 자 뺄 겁니다, 앞으로 쭉.
examples.trans: I am going to drop the honorific suffix—from now on, all the way.
I thought it over again (continuously, all the way).

meanings.note: 처음부터 means 'from the start'

examples.trans: Let's start over from the beginning.
This is my first time coming to Seoul.

meanings.note: Used in spoken Korean dialogue (verb).

examples.trans: I have lived here ever since I was born.

meanings.en: to do, to perform, to hold
meanings.note: Core verb; also combines with nouns to form verbs.

examples.trans: What are you doing right now?
We are holding a meeting today.
